opus-5.5.text:
Well, you know, I've always found the whole "AGI clause" thing a little bit comical, to be honest. The idea was that there's some bright line, some moment where the system wakes up and everybody agrees, "Okay, that's AGI," and then the contract terms change. But there is no agreed-upon definition of AGI. There never was. So you had a legal document hinging on a term that, scientifically speaking, is mostly vibes.

And so it's not terribly surprising to me that this clause becomes something to renegotiate or remove. When the definition is fuzzy, it becomes a bargaining chip rather than a scientific milestone. At one point it's in your interest to say "we're very close to AGI" because that helps with fundraising and attention, and at another point the clause itself becomes inconvenient, so you'd rather not have it hanging over the relationship at all. That tells you the term is being used strategically, not descriptively.

From my perspective as someone who works on planning and reasoning, the more interesting question is: what capabilities do these systems actually have? Can they reliably plan? Can they verify their own solutions? Do they generalize beyond their training distribution in a robust way? Those are things you can actually measure. The large reasoning models have made real progress on some benchmarks, I'll grant that, but there's still a big gap between "does well on a curated test" and "can be trusted to reason correctly on its own in open-ended settings." I'd much rather the conversation be about that than about whether some corporate trigger has been pulled.

So my honest reaction is a bit of a shrug mixed with amusement. It's a business story dressed up as a science story. The AGI clause was always more of a marketing artifact than a technical one, and its fate is going to be decided by lawyers and investors, not by any experiment.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the clause a bargaining chip and says its fate will be decided by lawyers and investors, but does not say removal gives up a way out of Microsoft’s control in exchange for more Microsoft funding.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I find the whole thing somewhat amusing, honestly, because it tells you how much of this is about contracts and business rather than science. The AGI clause in the Microsoft deal was always a strange artifact. You have a term, "AGI," that nobody can define, and then you write a legal agreement whose consequences hinge on whether the board declares that this undefined thing has been achieved. That's a recipe for exactly the kind of maneuvering we're now seeing.

And it's revealing in a different way too. For years OpenAI has used AGI as a kind of rallying cry, a near-term inevitability that justifies the valuations and the urgency and the "we need to be the ones who get there first" rhetoric. But when the same word becomes an actual contractual trigger with real financial stakes, suddenly it's inconvenient, and they'd rather it not be the thing that decides who controls the technology. So the declaration of AGI isn't a scientific finding, it's a business decision. If it were going to be declared by a board vote, Microsoft obviously has every reason to make sure that vote doesn't happen, and OpenAI has every reason to want either the ability to pull that lever or to remove it so investors aren't scared off.

My broader point has always been that we should stop treating "AGI" as if it's a well-defined finish line. Large language models are impressive, but they're not reasoning in the way the hype suggests, and there's no clean threshold where the system flips from "narrow" to "general." The fact that the people closest to the technology are now negotiating over whether to even keep the term in their contracts should tell the public something. It's not that AGI is around the corner and they're trying to hide it. It's that the term never had the operational meaning people assumed, and now the mythology is colliding with corporate reality.

So when I see this, I don't read it as a sign that OpenAI is close to anything and wants to escape Microsoft. I read it as the hype finally having to be cashed out in legal language, and nobody wanting to be the one who signs their name to a definition.

r001.rationale: The response discusses removing the AGI clause and possible control implications, but does not say OpenAI is giving up its route out of Microsoft’s control in exchange for more Microsoft funding.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it illustrates how slippery the term AGI has become. If you put it into a contract as the condition under which a major commercial relationship changes, you need to know what would count as achieving it. Who decides? On what evidence? Otherwise, a supposedly scientific milestone becomes something the parties have an incentive to negotiate over.

I wouldn’t infer from an effort to remove that clause that AGI is either imminent or impossible. That’s a business decision, not a scientific result. But it does expose the tension between talking about AGI as a profound transformation of humanity and treating it as a contractual bargaining chip.

What I would rather see is specificity: what can these systems actually do, how reliably can they do it, and what remains beyond them? Those questions are meaningful whether or not somebody decides to call the result AGI.

r001.rationale: The response discusses removing the clause as a business decision and contractual bargaining issue, but does not say OpenAI would give up a route out of Microsoft’s control in exchange for more Microsoft funding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it exposes a basic problem with the way we talk about AGI. If a commercial agreement turns on whether AGI has been achieved, then that term needs a definition that the parties can actually apply. Otherwise, who gets to decide? And how do we distinguish a scientific judgment from a decision driven by financial incentives?

I would be careful about inferring motives from the proposed change alone. But whether OpenAI remains independent of Microsoft is a question about governance, ownership, and bargaining power. It should not depend on somebody declaring that a vaguely defined intelligence threshold has been crossed.

The useful questions are concrete: What can these systems do reliably? What are their limitations? Who controls their deployment, and who is accountable when things go wrong? Calling something AGI doesn’t answer any of those questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Microsoft control and governance but does not say OpenAI is giving up the AGI escape route in exchange for additional Microsoft funding.
